claim_text: Marcus Antonius was born on 14 January 83 BCE in Rome.
status_note: Birth year disputed. Plutarch records age 53 or 56 at death (Plut. Ant. 86.5). 83 BCE derived from Cicero Phil. 2.24 reference to quaestorship age.

claim_text: Antony served as praefectus equitum (cavalry commander) under Aulus Gabinius in Syria and Egypt in 57–55 BCE.
Antony served as a military officer under Julius Caesar during the Gallic Wars from 54 to 50 BCE.
Antony was elected Tribune of the Plebs for the year 49 BCE.
When Antony's tribunician veto against the senatus consultum ultimum was ignored, he fled Rome to join Caesar at Ravenna in January 49 BCE, triggering open civil war.
Antony commanded the left wing of Caesar's army at the Battle of Pharsalus in 48 BCE.
Caesar appointed Antony as Magister Equitum (Master of Horse) in 48–47 BCE, making him Caesar's second-in-command in Italy while Caesar campaigned in the East.
Caesar chose Antony as his consular colleague for the year 44 BCE.
Antony publicly offered a royal diadem to Caesar three times at the Lupercalia festival on 15 February 44 BCE.
status_note: Attested by multiple sources including Cicero (Phil. 2.85-87) and Plut. Ant. 12. Interpretations of Antony's motive vary.

claim_text: Antony delivered the funeral oration for Caesar in March 44 BCE, reading Caesar's will and displaying the blood-stained toga to the crowd.
Antony secured possession of Caesar's state papers and treasury after the assassination, giving him significant political leverage in April–May 44 BCE.
Antony besieged Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus at Mutina in 43 BCE, leading the Senate to declare Antony a public enemy.
Antony formed the Second Triumvirate with Octavian and Lepidus as triumviri rei publicae constituendae, ratified by the Lex Titia in November 43 BCE.
The triumvirs published proscription lists in late 43 BCE, executing approximately 300 senators and 2,000 equites, including Cicero.
status_note: Exact numbers differ between sources. Appian Civil Wars 4.5 gives c. 300 senators and 2,000 equites.

claim_text: Antony played the leading military role in defeating Brutus and Cassius at the two engagements of the Battle of Philippi in October 42 BCE.
status_note: Antony won the first battle; Octavian was reportedly ill. The second battle completed the victory.

claim_text: Antony met Cleopatra VII in Tarsus, Cilicia, in 41 BCE.
Antony spent the winter of 41–40 BCE in Alexandria with Cleopatra VII.
Antony's brother Lucius Antonius and wife Fulvia waged the Perusine War against Octavian in Italy, 41–40 BCE.
status_note: Antony's own involvement or direction is disputed. Appian suggests Fulvia and Lucius acted with Antony's knowledge; others argue they acted independently.

claim_text: Antony agreed the Pact of Brundisium with Octavian in 40 BCE, dividing the Roman territories: Antony received the East, Octavian the West, Lepidus Africa.
Antony married Octavia Minor, Octavian's sister, in 40 BCE.
Antony fathered two daughters, Antonia Major and Antonia Minor, with Octavia.
Antony renewed the triumvirate for a further five years at the Pact of Tarentum in 37 BCE.
Antony's Parthian campaign of 36 BCE resulted in heavy Roman losses and a retreat without taking the Parthian capital.
status_note: Plutarch estimates 20,000 infantry and 4,000 cavalry lost (Plut. Ant. 44-51).

claim_text: Antony captured the Armenian king Artavasdes II in 34 BCE, presenting him to Cleopatra as a prisoner.
Antony conducted the Donations of Alexandria in 34 BCE, proclaiming Cleopatra's children as rulers of eastern Roman territories and client kingdoms.
status_note: The ceremony assigned titles to Cleopatra as 'Queen of Kings', Caesarion as 'King of Kings', and territories to Alexander Helios, Cleopatra Selene, and Ptolemy Philadelphus.

claim_text: Octavian obtained what he claimed was Antony's will from the Vestal Virgins and read its contents to the Senate in 32 BCE.
status_note: The will may have been forged or altered by Octavian. The contents reportedly included confirmation of the Donations of Alexandria and a wish to be buried in Alexandria with Cleopatra.

claim_text: Antony formally divorced Octavia in 32 BCE.
The Roman Senate declared war on Cleopatra VII and stripped Antony of his triumviral powers and future consulship in 32 BCE.
status_note: Octavian framed the war as against Cleopatra (a foreign enemy) rather than Antony (a Roman citizen), avoiding the appearance of renewed civil war.

claim_text: Antony's fleet was defeated by Octavian's admiral Agrippa at the naval Battle of Actium on 2 September 31 BCE.
Cleopatra's squadron withdrew during the Battle of Actium and Antony followed her with approximately 40 ships, abandoning his fleet.
status_note: Whether this was a pre-arranged plan or panic is disputed among ancient and modern historians.

claim_text: Antony's remaining land legions in Greece surrendered to Octavian after a week-long standoff in 31 BCE.
Antony committed suicide by falling on his sword in Alexandria on 1 August 30 BCE.
According to Plutarch, Antony died in Cleopatra's arms after being hauled up to her mausoleum (Plut. Ant. 77).
status_note: The dramatic death scene may be embellished by Plutarch's source tradition. Cassius Dio 51.10-11 gives a similar but not identical account.

claim_text: Octavian ordered a damnatio memoriae against Antony: his statues were removed, his name erased from inscriptions, and his birthday declared a dies vitiosus (ill-omened day).
status_note: The damnatio was partial: some inscriptions survive. The ban on the praenomen Marcus in the gens Antonia was lifted later.

claim_text: Antony has been characterized as Cleopatra's lover overwhelmed by eastern decadence, a portrayal largely shaped by Augustan propaganda (the 'inimici' tradition).
status_note: This is a received image from Augustan-era sources such as the poets Horace (Epode 9, Odes 1.37) and Virgil (Aeneid 8) and the hostile tradition used by Plutarch, Appian, and Cassius Dio. Modern scholarship distinguishes the historical Antony from this propaganda.
